this appeal by special leave is directed against the decision dated april 24 1950 of the central government industrial tribunal at dhanbad companyfirming the decision dated february 2 1950 of the regional labour companymissioner  central  dhanbad which had declared the one-day strike by the appellant the took place on numberember 7 1949 to be an illegal strike. the relevant facts are as follows - 

on october 13 1949 the appellants through the secretary of their union gave a numberice to the respondents under section 22 1  of the industrial disputes act 1947 that they proposed to call a one-day strike on the expiry of numberember 6 1949 for the fulfilment of demands 16 in number numbered therein. this strike numberice was in accordance with rule 85 of the rules framed under the industrial disputes act 1947 sent to  1  the companyciliation officer  central  dhanbad  2  the regional labour companymissioner  central  dhanbad  3  the chief labour companymissioner department of labour government of india new delhi  4  secretary ministry of labour government of india new delhi and  5  a. d. c. dhanbad. this numberice was received at the office of the regional labour companymissioners  central  dhanbad on october 15 1949. the regional labour companymissioner  central  held companyciliation proceedings at dhanbad on october 22 1949 but the appellants by their letter of same date declined the participate in the proceedings alleging that they were companyvinced that numberhing would companye out of the same and that the proceedings should therefore be companysidered to be ceased. on the same day the regional labour companymissioner  central  dhanbad addressed letter number rlc company 5  token  7910 to the chief labour companymissioner new delhi stating that after receipt of the numberice of strike he had issued numberice to the parties of companyciliation that the employers representatives were ready to discuss the demands but the unions representative filed a petition in writing saying that they did number want to participate in the proceedings and that numberfresh material had been placed before him to change his view and he was number in favour of recommending a reference of the demand to the industrial tribunal. the letter ended with a request that the government may be informed of the situation. it appears that this report was received in the office of the chief labour companymissioner new delhi on october 25 1949. although the chief labour companymissioner in his letter of numberember 17 1949 to the regional labour companymissioner  central  dhanbad states that the companytents of the latters report had already been companymunicated to the ministry of labour a companyy of the report was actually sent to and received by the ministry of labour only on that day. in the meantime on numberember 7 1949 the appellants about 700 in number went on one-day strike as per their strike numberice. apparently the respondents companytended that the strike was illegal and they made an application under section 8 2  of the companyl mines provident fund and bonus scheme act 1948 to the regional labour companymissioner  central  dhanbad for a decision on the question whether the strike was legal or illegal. by his order dated february 2 1950 the regional labour companymissioner  central  dhanbad declared that the strike was illegal. being aggrieved by the aforesaid decision the appellants under section 8 4  of the last mentioned act preferred an appeal to the central government industrial tribunal at dhanbad which however also held that the strike was illegal and that the companyclusions arrived at by the regional labour companymissioner  central  were companyrect and accordingly dismissed the appeal. the appellants thereafter applied for and obtained special leave to appeal to this companyrt. the only question raised on this appeal is whether the strike was illegal. section 24 1  of the act provides inter alia that a strike shall be illegal if it is companymenced or declared in companytravention of section 22 or section 23 of the act. section 22 1  provides as follows - 

22.  1  numberperson employed in a public utility service shall go on strike in breach of companytract - 

 a  without giving to the employer numberice of strike as hereinafter provided within six weeks before striking or 

 b  within fourteen days of giving such numberice or 

 c  before the expiry of the date of strike specified in any such numberice as aforesaid or 

 d  during the pendency of any companyciliation proceedings before a companyciliation officer and seven days after the companyclusion of such proceedings. numberice of strike having been given in terms of clause  a  and 14 days having elapsed after the giving of such numberice as required by clause  b  and the actual strike having taken place after numberember 6 1949 being the date specified in the strike numberice the only other question for companysideration is whether the strike took place during the pendency of any companyciliation proceedings before a companyciliation officer and seven days after the companyclusion of such proceedings. under section 20 1  a companyciliation proceeding shall be deemed to have companymenced on the date on which a numberice of strike under section 22 is received by the companyciliation officer. in this case the strike numberice was received by the regional labour companymissioner  central  who is the companyciliation officer on october 15 1949 and the companyciliation proceedings therefore companymenced on that date under section 20 1 . the relevant portion of sub-section  2  of that section runs as follows - 

a companyciliation proceeding shall be deemed to have companycluded - 

 a   

 b  where numbersettlement is arrived at when the report of the companyciliation officer is received by the appropriate government or when the report of the board is published under section 17 as the case may be or 

 c   

the regional labour companymissioner  central  who is the companyciliation officer in this dispute is required by section 12 to hold companyciliation proceedings in the prescribed manner and without delay investigate the dispute and to do all such things as he thinks fit for the purpose of inducing the parties to companye to a fair and amicable settlement of the dispute. in this case the regional labour companymissioner  central  held companyciliation proceedings on october 22 1949 but numbersettlement companyld be arrived at as the appellants declined to take part in the proceedings on the ground that they were companyvinced that numberhing would companye out of it. that being the position under section 12 4  it became the duty of the regional labour companymissioner  central  to as soon as practicable after the close of the investigation send to the appropriate government a full report setting forth the steps taken by him for ascertaining the facts and circumstances relating to the dispute and for bringing about a settlement thereof together with a full statement of such facts and circumstances and the reasons on account of which in this case a settlement companyld number be arrived at. sub-section  6  of this section requires that the report shall be submitted within fourteen days of the companymencement of the companyciliation proceedings or within such shorter period as may be fixed by the appropriate government. as already stated the companyciliation proceedings companymenced on october 15 1949. the report therefore was to be submitted within fourteen days from that date. in point of fact the report was sent by the regional labour companymissioner  central  to the chief labour companymissioner new delhi on october 22 1949  which was well within 14 days from the companymencement of the companyciliation proceedings  with the request that the government may be informed of the situation. under sub-section  4  the report has to be sent to the appropriate government which according to the definition under section 2 a  means in relation to an industrial dispute companycerning a mine the central government. the regional labour companymissioner  central  did number send the report direct to central government but sent it to the chief labour companymissioner new delhi in accordance with what has been called the usual companyrse and routine of official business. the report however was received by the central government on or about numberember 17 1949 and it is only on such receipt that the companyciliation proceedings are to be deemed to have companycluded according to the provisions of section 20 2  b . prima facie therefore the strike which took place on numberember 7 1949 was during the pendency of the companyciliation proceedings as held by the authorities below. shri n. c. chatterjee however argues that in point of fact the companyciliation proceedings came to an end when the appellants had withdrawn from the proceedings and the regional labour companymissioner  central  had sent his report. it is by a legal fiction introduced by section 20 2  b  that the companyciliation proceedings are prolonged until the actual receipt of the report by the appropriate government. according to shri n. c. chatterjee the companyciliation proceedings should be held to terminate when the regional labour companymissioner  central  sent his report within fourteen days of the companymencement of the companyciliation proceedings. the difficulty in accepting this argument is that while the word send is used in section 12 4  and the word submitted in section 12 6  the word used in section 20 2  b  is received. that word obviously implies the actual receipt of the report. to say that the companyciliation proceedings shall be deemed to have companycluded when the report should in the ordinary companyrse of business have been received by the appropriate government would introduce an element of uncertainty for the provisions of section 22 1  d  clearly companytemplate that the appropriate government should have a clear seven days time after the companyclusion of the companyciliation proceedings to make up its mind as to the further steps it should take. it is therefore necessary that the beginning of the seven days time should be fixed so that there would be certainty as to when the seven days time would expire. it is therefore provided in section 20 2  b  that the proceedings shall be deemed to have companycluded where numbersettlement is arrived at when the report is actually received by the appropriate government. shri n. c. chatterjee on the other hand strongly urges and number without some force that on that companystruction it may be possible for the government or its officers to withhold the report designedly or the report may be lost in companyrse of transit or may be actually received after the expiry of the date fixed for the strike in the numberice under section 22 1 . shri n. c. chatterjee also points out that it will number be possible for the workers to knumber when the report is actually received and their right to strike may thus be taken away from them. shri n. c. chatterjee companytends that the government cannumber take advantage of its own wrong. while we feel companysiderable force in shri n. c. chatterjees argument based on hardship we are bound to assume that the public officers companycerned would act fairly and properly. further it is number a case of the government taking advantage of its own wrong as suggested by shri n. c. chatterjee for here we are companycerned with a dispute between the employers and the employees and there is numbermaterial before us to justify our attributing the misdeeds if any of the regional labour companymissioner  central  or of the chief labour companymissioner to the respondents the employers who are entitled to take their stand on the language of the law. the companyrt can only companystrue the statute as it finds it and if there is any defect in the law it is for other authority than this companyrt to rectify the same. shri n. c. chatterjee also urges that the regional labour companymissioner  central  should have under section 12 sent his report to the appropriate government which in this case means the central government and he should number have sent the report to the chief labour companymissioner. assuming that that is the position then the fact will still remain that the central government did number receive the report and therefore the companyciliation proceedings did number companye to an end when the strike took place. shri n. c. chatterjee also suggests that the chief labour companymissioner should have returned the report to the regional labour companymissioner  central  because under the law the report should number have been made to him. he however did number return the same to the regional companymissioner but took upon himself to forward the same to the labour ministry. in the circumstances shri n. c. chatterjee urges on the authority of chaturbhuj ram lal v. secretary of state for india  that the chief labour companymissioner must be deemed to be the agent of the central government for the purpose of receiving the report. we adjourned this case in order to enable shri n. c. chatterjee to ascertain whether there was any delegation of authority in this behalf by the central government to the chief labour companymissioner. shri n. c. chatterjee has number been able to discover any such delegation of authority. it seems obvious to us that the chief labour companymissioner cannumber possibly be regarded for this purpose as the central government. in point of fact by a numberification in the gazette of india dated april 5 1947 the chief labour companymissioner has been appointed as a companyciliation officer and therefore in companyciliation proceedings companyducted by him he has to submit his report to the central government. it follows therefore that the chief labour companymissioner must be an authority separate from the central government. according to rule 85 to which reference has been made the strike numberice has to be sent amongst others to the chief labour companymissioner as well as to the department of labour of the government of india which again indicates that the two are different entities. the chief labour companymissioner is therefore only the channel or post office through which companyrespondence between the regional labour companymissioner  central  and the central government is to pass and he cannumber possibly be regarded as an agent of the central government for the purpose of receiving the report. the chief labour companymissioner being the official channel the ruling relied upon by shri n. c. chatterjee can have numberapplication to the facts of this case. for reasons stated above we are of opinion that the companyclusions arrived at by the authorities below on this point are companyrect and that this appeal must be dismissed. in the peculiar circumstances of the case however we think that there should be numberorder as to companyts and the parties should bear their own companyts. before companycluding we must draw the attention of the authorities companycerned to the slack and unbusiness-like manner in which the matter was dealt with in the office of the chief labour companymissioner. the act requires that the companyciliation officer must submit his report within 14 days from the companymencement of companyciliation proceedings and then on receipt of the report by the appropriate government the companyciliation proceedings are to be deemed to have companycluded. although factually the companyciliation proceedings terminate when a settlement is arrived at before the companyciliation officer or when it is found that numbersettlement can be arrived at the act by a legal fiction prolongs the companyciliation proceedings until the actual receipt of the report by the appropriate government and goes on to provide that the appropriate government must have seven days time to companysider what further steps it would take under the act. up to the expiry of this period of 7 days the act permits numberstrike but after that period is over the employees are left free to resort to companylective action by way of a strike. indeed it is on the basis of these provisions that the date of strike has to be carefully selected and specified in the numberice of strike to be given by the employees under section 22 1  of the act. thus even a cursory perusal of the act makes it clear that time is of the essence of the act and that the requirements of its relevant provisions must be punctually obeyed and carried out if the act is to operate harmoniously at all. in this case the companyciliation officer submitted his report on october 22 1949 i.e. well within 14 days from the companymencement of the companyciliation proceedings as required by section 12 6  of the act. the report was sent through what has been called the routine official channel. admittedly it was received in the office of the chief labour companymissioner at new delhi on october 25 1949 but surprisingly it was number passed on to the ministry of labour which is also in new delhi until about numberember 17 1949. the employees had numbermeans of knumbering when the report was actually received by the central government which is the appropriate government in this case or when the period of 7 days after such receipt expired.

shri c. k. daphtary also fails.
